_note: Original advanced lesson. Uses language-specific block variants where syntax differs.
title: Hash Maps & Sets
summary: Use a **set** to remember what you have seen. Use a **map** when each **key** needs a value, such as a count.
refresher: A **set** answers membership questions: have I seen this value before? A **map** stores a value for each **key**, such as a frequency count. Both are useful when repeated scanning would be too slow.

advanced-set-membership.title: Sets answer seen-before questions
advanced-set-membership.body: A **set** stores unique **values** and lets you check membership quickly.
advanced-set-membership.example: if value in seen: return True
advanced-set-membership.notice: You care whether the **value** exists, not how many times.
advanced-set-membership.mistake: Using a **list** works, but each lookup can scan the whole list.

advanced-map-counts.title: Maps attach a value to each key
advanced-map-counts.body: A frequency **map** uses the item as the **key** and the count as the **value**.
advanced-map-counts.notice: The **key** is what you look up. The **value** is what you store about it.
advanced-map-counts.mistake: Increasing a missing **key** before creating it causes errors in many languages.

advanced-map-default.title: Start missing counts at zero
advanced-map-default.body: Before you add one, decide what a missing **key** should mean. For counts, missing usually means zero.
advanced-map-default.notice: The default prevents a missing-**key** crash.
advanced-map-default.mistake: Do not assume every **key** already exists.

sections.title: Set: remember unique values
sections.summary: A **set** is for fast yes-or-no membership checks.

blocks.body: Use a **set** when the question asks whether a **value** appeared before, whether duplicates exist, or whether two groups share values. A set does not care about order or counts. It cares about membership.

blocks.title: Check membership before adding
blocks.caption: Watch a **set** answer “have I seen this before?” without counting every **value**.

steps.title: Read 4
steps.what_changed: After the check, add 4 so future **values** can compare against it.

steps.title: Read 7
steps.body: 7 is also missing, so add it.

steps.title: Read 4 again
steps.body: 4 is already in the **set**, so this is the repeat.
steps.what_changed: The **set** gives a yes/no answer without scanning the earlier **list** by hand.

blocks.caption: A duplicate checker looks before it adds.

blocks.title: Check before adding
blocks.body: If you add first, the current **value** will always look seen. That makes every value look like a duplicate.

blocks.prompt: Why does the duplicate checker test membership before adding the **value**?
choices: So the current value does not count as its own duplicate
So duplicates are removed from the input
blocks.why: The **set** should only contain earlier **values**. That is why the check comes first.

sections.title: Map: store a value for each key
sections.summary: A **map** is for relationships like item -> count.

blocks.body: Use a **map** when one piece of data needs another piece attached to it. In a frequency map, the **key** is the item and the **value** is how many times it appears.

blocks.title: Lookup before insert
blocks.caption: Watch a **map** use a missing-**key** default before it updates a count.

steps.title: Read b
steps.body: b is missing, so its old count acts like 0.
steps.what_changed: The new count becomes 1 and is stored under **key** b.

steps.title: Read a
steps.body: a is missing too, so it starts at 1.

steps.title: Read a again
steps.body: a already exists, so read the old **value** and add one.
steps.what_changed: The **key** stays a. Only the **value** changes from 1 to 2.

blocks.title: Track counts with a map
blocks.caption: Watch a frequency table change as **values** are read.

steps.title: Read cat
steps.body: cat is not in the table yet, so its count starts at 1.

steps.title: Read dog
steps.body: dog gets its own **key** with count 1.

steps.title: Read cat again
steps.body: cat is already a **key**, so update its old **value**.

blocks.caption: Count frequencies by reading each item once.

blocks.title: Read the update pattern
items: Use zero if the **key** is missing.
Store the new count back under the same **key**.

blocks.title: C++ note
blocks.body: `counts[ch] += 1` creates the **key** with **value** `0` if it is missing, then adds one. That is convenient for counts.

blocks.prompt: In a frequency **map** for course codes, what is the **key**?
blocks.why: The **key** is the thing you look up. The count is the **value** stored for that key.

sections.title: Handle missing keys and collisions calmly
sections.summary: Map code needs a missing-key rule before it can update a saved value.

blocks.body: A map lookup has two questions. Does the key already exist? If it does, use or update the saved value. If it does not, choose a default before doing arithmetic or appending.

blocks.title: Lookup, default, update
blocks.caption: Watch a key land in a bucket, then either reuse an entry or create one.

steps.title: Read key
steps.body: The key is the value used for lookup.

steps.title: Choose bucket
steps.body: The hash function decides which bucket to inspect.

steps.title: Key appears again
steps.body: Use the existing entry instead of making a duplicate key.

steps.title: Update saved value
steps.body: The value for that key changes from 1 to 2.

blocks.prompt: Why choose a default before adding to a missing count?
choices: There is no old number to add to yet
The key must be deleted first
All counts must start at one hundred
The map becomes a set automatically
blocks.why: A missing key has no saved count, so the code needs a starting value such as zero before incrementing.

sections.title: Choose the right one
sections.summary: Ask whether you need a count or only membership.

blocks.caption: **Sets** and **maps** solve different questions.
blocks.wrong: Use a set when you need counts: seen.add(code)
blocks.right: Use a map when you need counts: counts[code] += 1
blocks.body: A **set** can say a code appeared. A **map** can say how many times.

blocks.title: Quick decision rule
items: Need counts, positions, or labels? Use a **map**.
Need order too? Use the language's ordered structure or store a **list** as well.

blocks.prompt: You need to know whether a name appears at least once. Which structure is enough?
blocks.why: A **set** is enough because the question only asks whether the name exists.

blocks.body: When a **map** question feels messy, draw a two-column table: **key** on the left, value on the right. Update one row per **loop** step.

blocks.title: Do not mix up keys and values
blocks.body: If the prompt asks for the most common **value**, the answer may be a **key**. The count is only evidence you use to choose it.
